Gene Kranz. American aerospace engineer and flight director who led NASA Mission Control during the Apollo program, most notably during the Apollo 13 crisis. Though not a rocket designer in the von Braun mold, Kranz was the operational brain that commanded the Space Race from the ground.

He served as Flight Director for Apollo 11, Apollo 12, and Apollo 13 — the three most critical moments of the lunar landing program. His calm authority and decision-making under pressure became legend. Kranz pioneered the role of Flight Director as a leader who integrates hundreds of specialists into a single coordinated mission, making life-or-death decisions in real time.

During Apollo 13 in April 1970, when an oxygen tank exploded, Kranz orchestrated the improvised solution to bring the spacecraft safely home — a feat celebrated as a triumph of engineering and human ingenuity. He developed the "Failure Is Not an Option" ethos at NASA, a culture of meticulous checklist discipline, redundancy, and relentless problem-solving that defined American spaceflight. Kranz trained and mentored generations of flight controllers and operations personnel, and his leadership style became the model for high-reliability organizations worldwide.

He authored the memoir Failure Is Not an Option in 2000, which chronicles the human side of the Space Race and Apollo.
